Mmm... this is a bit too simplistic for my tastes, but it's fundamentally true, at least in our current world. It's also why my own preference is for capitalism. And, for that matter, for anarchism. They're both expressions of the same fundamental idea - society is not truly a single collective entity. It is, instead, the sum of the norms and values and beliefs and decisions of all of the individual actors that make it up. Therefore, obviously the most efficient and effective way to most ensure that each and all of those individual actors have the greatest opportunity for satisfying lives is to seek to ensure that each and all of them are free to choose the norms and values and beliefs and decisions they prefer.

However, that immediately runs into the fact that some number of those individuals are going to wish to choose, among other things, to live under a socialistic economic system. They must be free to do so. Others must be free to not do so. And so on...

The biggest problems with the public opinion of both systems is that there are no perfect examples to look to.

People point to economic failures in America as a reason capitalism won't work. The problem with that is the US isn't running a purely capitalist system, but a bastardized version of it. For instance, bailing out banks & companies is the opposite of capitalism.

People point to economic failures in Europe as proof socialism doesn't work. But Europe isn't using a purely socialist system, but a bastardized version of it.

When capitalism is done correctly, it lifts more people out of poverty than socialism. The problem is not that capitalism can't work, it's that we're doing it wrong, purposefully, in order to maintain the status quo power structure. True capitalism would require constant evolution of our economic means (meaning some companies fail and other, better run companies succeed in their place), but that ebb/flow is not in the best interest of rich stockholders, so they're currently preventing it by employing anti-capitalist machinations.

Summary: true capitalism is extremely darwinian, but we're essentially keeping the dinosaurs on life-support instead of letting them die

People who like socialism find an appeal in the concept of taking care of one another and using the government to pay for the things that people need.

People who dislike socialism have an understanding of applied economics and understand that you can't centrally plan prosperity. Socialism requires you to be heavily taxed and regulated to provide for things like universal college education. But when college education is subsidized then universities will hike up prices indefinitely. (The current skyrocketing tuition crisis is fueled by similar subsidies in the form of loose student loan policies.) So socialism prescribes price controls on education. But then the only way for a college to be more profitable than another college is for it to cut costs while enrolling as many (read: unqualified) students as possible. Then you're pumping out degrees in basketweaving (metaphorically) that have no worth in the real world -- the quality of everyone's education suffers -- and college becomes merely High School Part 2, with everyone throwing away four years of their life. So socialism prescribes state control of the educational process. But then as technology advances, education advances at the speed of bureacracy because once again the central planners haven't anticipated the needs of every individual American.

Every time you have a person or a group of people attempting to plan for the needs of the entire nation there will be some person or some contingency that hasn't been planned for. They can -- at best -- plan only for the "average" case. So -- on the whole -- you get a solution that fits a lot of people. But this creeps into every aspect of life: education, jobs, health care, etc. And on the whole your particular needs aren't quite met by the central planners in one or more areas. These problems build up, compound, and the system implodes. It has happened time and again throughout history. In the extreme case you get consequences that look a lot like what's going on in Venezuela right now -- with people starving while the government arrests the capitalists who are smuggling powdered milk across the border to feed people. In milder cases you get consequences like what's going on in Greece -- a bankrupt government, poverty, businesses emigrating to other jurisdictions.

People who oppose socialism aren't mean people who don't want others to go to college or have jobs or live a comfortable life. We're people who have studied economics, history and politics. And we understand that there are proven inefficiencies with these models and there are better ways to do things that lead to prosperity for everyone. For a brief but lengthier discussion of the consequences of various economic policies, I'd recommend reading "Economics in One Lesson" by Henry Hazlitt.
